country.comment: Primary fieldwork was conducted in two urban slums of Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh, India (Vajpayeenagar in Qutbullapur municipality and Banjara Colony in LB Nagar Municipality), as the India component of a multi-country project.
country.where_found: PDF p. 3, Abstract and Author Note; PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF p. 25, Acknowledgements

effect_estimate.comment: No quantitative point estimates, regressions, or statistical tests are reported for primary study outcomes; findings are synthesized qualitatively through resident interviews, focus group discussions, field observation, and illustrative task durations for 6 women (Table 2).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Comparing Vajpayeenagar (a notified slum eligible for all government development schemes, with piped water and VAMBAY pucca housing) and Banjara Colony (a non-notified slum with kutcha dwellings, salty handpumps, and tanker water), slum notification expanded access to housing and piped water schemes, yet uncoordinated scheme execution and poor municipal planning undermined sanitation access in both settlements: VAMBAY house construction demolished ILCS latrines built 1.5 years earlier without immediate replacement (forcing women to walk 0.5–1 km for open defecation), while top-down ILCS pit latrines lacked underground sewerage, overflowed and contaminated adjacent water tanks on black cotton soil during rains, could not be serviced along narrow lanes, and went unused in Banjara Colony until pucca latrines were linked to a new drainage system (alongside trickling individual taps) by July 2011.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF pp. 10–13, What is Appropriate Sanitation?, Box 2, and Everyone Wants a Personal Toilet; PDF pp. 24–25, A Summing Up

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the primary qualitative study design (CASP). Assigned 2 because fieldwork directly observed and documented the administrative and programmatic mechanisms operating on sanitation and water access—specifically slum notification eligibility, demolition of recent ILCS latrines during VAMBAY housing construction, and municipal failure to connect ILCS pit latrines to underground sewerage or include women in scheme planning and design.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF pp. 10–11, What is Appropriate Sanitation? and Box 2; PDF p. 24, A Summing Up

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines notified vs. non-notified slum status determining eligibility for government development schemes and permanent vs. nomadic settlement status (ELIGIBILITY: tenure), private landowners chasing women off private land during open defecation (property), poor municipal/technical planning of ILCS latrines on unsuitable soil without underground sewerage or lane access for vacuum tankers (planning), lack of inter-scheme coordination where VAMBAY housing demolished 1.5-year-old ILCS latrines and call for inter-sectoral convergence (institutional_fragmentation), and exclusion of poor women from top-down expert sanitation planning and decision-making (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: participation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, tenure, property, planning, participation, institutional_fragmentation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 3, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF pp. 10–12, What is Appropriate Sanitation? and Box 2; PDF pp. 24–25, A Summing Up

outcome_flags.comment: Examines access to and use of ILCS and private latrines vs. open defecation (sanitation_access), municipal piped, tanker, and handpump water (water_access), connection of latrines to underground sewerage and individual household water taps (formal_connection), salty unfiltered handpump water and pit seepage contaminating storage tanks plus overflowing/poorly designed latrines (service_quality), insufficient trickling tap water constraining bathing and menstrual hygiene (service_quantity), and household inability to afford Rs 5,000 private toilets, soap, or sanitary cleaners without government support (affordability).
outcome_flags.value: sanitation_access, water_access, formal_connection, service_quality, service_quantity, affordability
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 10–14, What is Appropriate Sanitation?, Box 2, Everyone Wants a Personal Toilet, and Hygiene and Hygienic Practices; PDF pp. 22–24, Menstruation and A Summing Up

publication_year.comment: Published in Indian Journal of Gender Studies, 18(3), 381–404 (2011), with Version of Record dated September 30, 2011 (note that running headers on PDF pp. 3, 6, 8, 9, and 17 contain a publisher typesetting artifact from another SAGE journal).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, cover page; PDF p. 2 ('Version of Record - Sep 30, 2011'); PDF p. 3, article citation block

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Although individual questionnaires are mentioned alongside guided-checklist household interviews, focus group discussions, and participatory observation, no quantitative survey sample size, dataset, or statistical analysis is reported; all empirical evidence presented is primary qualitative fieldwork, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the appropriate appraisal tool.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 7, Methodology; Table 1, PDF p. 6; Box 1, PDF pp. 8–9; Table 2, PDF p. 17

sample_size.comment: Authors selected 32 households stratified across 4 community-defined economic categories in 2 Hyderabad slums for in-depth guided-checklist household interviews, supplemented by focus group discussions (with women, adolescent girls, school-going children, and men), individual questionnaires, and direct observation; exact numbers of FGDs and individual questionnaire respondents are not reported (Table 2 profiles 6 women from poor households).
sample_size.value: 2 urban slums (total population ~4,913: ~2,413 in Vajpayeenagar and ~2,500 in Banjara Colony); 32 households (8 from each of 4 economic categories across both localities) for in-depth household interviews; focus group discussions (exact number of FGDs and participants not reported)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF p. 7, Methodology; Table 2, PDF p. 17

study_design.comment: Operationalized using Chambers' participatory approach and an Asset and Vulnerability framework to stratify households into 4 income/vulnerability categories across one notified slum and one non-notified slum, plus a July 2011 follow-up site visit; all reported empirical results are qualitative and descriptive.
study_design.value: Participatory qualitative field study in two urban slums (one notified, one non-notified) using guided-checklist in-depth household interviews, focus group discussions, individual questionnaires, and direct observation
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 5, Methodology; PDF p. 7, Methodology; PDF p. 24, A Summing Up
